newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends battered amid seasonal downtrend.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends battered amid seasonal downtrend.

text.p: NYMEX crude continued its sharp decline Friday as the need for refined product diminished amid declining heating oil use and the peak summer demand season for gasoline still too far away.

"We are in the proverbial "in between season" - it's too early for gasoline to help the market and it's too late for heating oil," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady, noting the nearest futures contracts now reflect the spring months.
March crude settled off 87 cents a barrel at $22.23, declining for the fourth consecutive session and losing $1.92 a barrel for the week.

Dealers cited heavy fund selling, with Energex named in particular. Energex declined comment. Sell stops were triggered after crude broke key psychological support of $23.00 for the first time in three months, traders said.
March heating oil ended off 0.92 cent at 60.53 cents a gallon while March gasoline ended off 2.24 cents at 63.06 cents a gallon.
Heating oil has lost more than eight cents a gallon since last Friday as temperatures have trended above normal in the northeastern United States, the largest heating oil market in the world.

Although the region was forecasted to experience colder weather next week, widely watched meteorologist Jon Davis of Smith Barney in Chicago said the cold snap would not be as strong as orginally expected.
Davis expected temperatures midweek to be four to eight degrees below normal in the region rather than eight to 12 degrees below normal.
"Even if it does get cold, refiners can simply dump the inventory they already have on the market," said O'Grady.

Indeed, refiners have more than ample heat supply, with the American Petroleum Institute (API) reporting Tuesday that distillate stocks, comprised of heating oil and diesel, showed a surplus for the first time in more than a year.
"The key here is that there is no demand for refined product. And we have plenty of gasoline coming in," said a New York trader.

Some market players were expecting gasoline imports to approach a historically high 650,000 barrels per day in February due in part to an open arbitrage from Europe in January. Gasoline demand, however, is traditionally poor in the winter.

Meanwhile, the defence minister of Ecuador, a leading oil producer, declared a nationwide state of emergency Friday to attempt to quell protests against President Abdala Bucaram, who was ousted by Congress on Thursday.
But, the market shrugged off the news since the political turmoil was reported not to be affecting the country's oil exports.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
